headline: UK public sector debt passes £3 trillion for the first time, ONS says

terms.meaning: The total the government owes, minus the cash and liquid assets it holds.
Government bonds whose payments rise with inflation, which makes debt interest costs go up when prices rise.

levels.headline: UK public sector debt passes £3 trillion for the first time, ONS says
levels.body:
UK public sector net debt passed £3 trillion for the first time, the Office for National Statistics (ONS) said on 21 October. Provisional figures put debt at £3,005.0 billion at the end of September 2026, equal to 94.0% of GDP.
Borrowing in September alone was £24.5 billion, which is £1.8 billion (7.7%) more than in September 2025 and £1.9 billion above the forecast of the Office for Budget Responsibility (OBR). The ONS said spending grew faster than tax receipts. About £4.0 billion reflected the uplift on index-linked gilts, largely because the Retail Prices Index rose 0.6% between June and July 2026.
In the financial year to September, borrowing was £97.8 billion. That is £4.4 billion (4.3%) lower than a year earlier but £6.0 billion above the OBR forecast. The figures arrive days before the Autumn Budget, scheduled for 28 October, when Chancellor John Healey must show how he will keep borrowing under control.
levels.why: It shows how little room the Chancellor has, which affects taxes, spending and the cost of borrowing for everyone.

levels.headline: UK public sector debt passes £3 trillion for the first time, ONS says
levels.body:
The UK's public sector net debt has gone above £3 trillion for the first time, according to the Office for National Statistics. It stood at £3,005.0 billion at the end of September, which is 94.0% of the size of the whole economy.
The government borrowed £24.5 billion in September alone. That was £1.8 billion more than a year earlier and £1.9 billion more than the official forecaster, the Office for Budget Responsibility, had expected. Spending grew faster than tax income, and debt interest rose partly because some government bonds are linked to inflation.
Over the first half of the financial year, borrowing totalled £97.8 billion, slightly less than a year ago but £6.0 billion above the forecast. The data comes just before the Budget on 28 October, when Chancellor John Healey will set out his plans.
levels.why: It shows how little room the Chancellor has, which affects taxes, spending and the cost of borrowing for everyone.

levels.headline: UK public sector debt passes £3 trillion for the first time, ONS says

Borrowing for the first six months of the financial year was £97.8 billion. The figures come days before the Budget on 28 October, when Chancellor John Healey will explain how he plans to manage the public finances.

levels.headline: UK public sector debt passes £3 trillion for the first time, ONS says

levels.headline: UK national debt passes £3 trillion for the first time

levels.headline: UK national debt passes £3 trillion for the first time
levels.body:
Britain's government has borrowed money for many years, and the total it owes has now passed £3 trillion. That is a number with twelve zeros. The Office for National Statistics counted it and told everyone on 21 October.
Think of it like a very big family credit card. Each month the government spends more than it earns from taxes, so it borrows a bit more. In September it borrowed £24.5 billion. It also pays interest on what it owes, and that cost went up.
On 28 October the Chancellor, John Healey, will make a big speech called the Budget. He will say how the government plans to collect and spend money. People will listen closely to what he says about the debt.

levels.headline: Britain's debt passes £3 trillion
levels.body:
The UK government owes a huge amount of money. This week we learned it has gone over £3 trillion. That is the first time. The Office for National Statistics, a group that counts things for the country, shared this on 21 October.
Governments borrow money to pay for things like hospitals and schools. In September they borrowed £24.5 billion more. They had planned to borrow less. They must also pay extra, called interest, for borrowing. Interest is like a fee for using someone else's money.
On 28 October the Chancellor, John Healey, will give a speech called the Budget. He will explain how the government will get and spend money. Taxes could change, so many families are waiting to hear.
levels.why: It matters because the government's money choices can change taxes, prices and what is spent on schools and hospitals.

levels.headline: Britain's debt passes £3 trillion
levels.body:
A country can owe money, just like a person can. The UK government has borrowed so much that it now owes over £3 trillion. That is the biggest it has ever been. People who count the country's money told us on 21 October.
Why does the government borrow? It pays for hospitals, schools and roads. When it spends more than it gets from taxes, it borrows the rest. In September it borrowed £24.5 billion. It also pays interest, which is a small extra charge for borrowing.
On 28 October the Chancellor will explain the plan for money in a big speech called the Budget. It could change what people pay in tax. That is why people are watching.
levels.why: It matters because the government's money choices can change taxes, prices and what is spent on schools and hospitals.

levels.headline: Britain's debt passes £3 trillion
levels.body:
Imagine your class has a big jar of money for trips and treats. But the teacher keeps borrowing from the jar, and now owes it a lot. The UK government is a bit like that, but with much bigger numbers. It now owes over £3 trillion.
The government spends money on schools, hospitals and roads. It gets money from taxes, which grown-ups pay. This month it spent more than it got, so it borrowed more. It also pays a little extra for borrowing, called interest.
On 28 October, the grown-up in charge of money, called the Chancellor, will say what happens next. We will find out soon whether things change.
levels.why: It matters because the government's money choices can change taxes, prices and what is spent on schools and hospitals.

headline: Wall Street: S&P 500 falls 1.21% to 7,663.43 as AI spending worries hit tech

terms.meaning: An index tracking 500 of the largest companies listed in the United States.
An index dominated by technology companies.

levels.headline: Wall Street: S&P 500 falls 1.21% to 7,663.43 as AI spending worries hit tech
levels.body:
The S&P 500 closed down on Thursday 22 October, the last completed session, falling 1.21% to 7,663.43. It was the index's worst day since July. The Nasdaq Composite dropped 2.6% to 26,008.86, its worst session since June, while the Dow Jones Industrial Average edged up 0.02% to 52,867.98, a gain of 11.89 points.
CNBC attributed the sell-off to renewed worries about how much artificial intelligence companies are spending, alongside a jump in oil prices on rising geopolitical tension. Technology shares led the decline, with Caterpillar down 4.99%, Amazon down 4.62% and Nvidia down 4.46% among the biggest fallers on the Dow list.
Homebuilders, regional banks and real estate investment trusts did better as bond yields slid. Investors are also watching the Federal Reserve's next decision on 28 October.
levels.why: Share prices affect pensions, savings and company investment, and tech wobbles can spread to markets worldwide.

headline: Bank of England expected to raise Bank Rate on 5 November after inflation hits 3.5%

terms.meaning: The Bank of England's main interest rate, which influences mortgage and savings rates.
Inflation leaving out volatile items such as energy and food.

levels.headline: Bank of England expected to raise Bank Rate on 5 November after inflation hits 3.5%
levels.body:
Markets now widely expect the Bank of England to raise interest rates at its meeting on 5 November, after UK inflation rose to 3.5% in the 12 months to September from 3.1% in August. The Office for National Statistics said the figure was above the 3.4% economists had forecast.
Bank Rate stands at 3.75%, against an inflation target of 2%. In September the Monetary Policy Committee voted 6-3 to hold, with three members backing a quarter-point rise to 4%. Core inflation edged up to 2.8% and services inflation to 3.7%. Motor fuel prices were 29.8% higher than a year earlier, which analysts link to the conflict involving the United States and Iran and disruption near the Strait of Hormuz.
CNBC reported that, according to LSEG data, markets put the chance of a rise on 5 November at around 98%, with a further increase possible in December.
levels.why: It affects mortgage payments, savings rates and the cost of borrowing for households and businesses.

levels.headline: Bank of England expected to raise Bank Rate on 5 November after inflation hits 3.5%
levels.body:
The Bank of England is widely expected to raise interest rates on 5 November. Inflation climbed to 3.5% in September, up from 3.1% in August and above the 3.4% economists expected, the Office for National Statistics reported.
The Bank's main rate is 3.75%, and its target for inflation is 2%. At its September meeting, six members of the Monetary Policy Committee voted to keep rates unchanged, while three wanted a rise of a quarter of a percentage point. Core inflation, which strips out energy and food, rose to 2.8%, and services inflation to 3.7%. Fuel prices were 29.8% higher than a year earlier.
Market pricing cited by CNBC suggests a rise next month is close to certain, with another possible in December.
levels.why: It affects mortgage payments, savings rates and the cost of borrowing for households and businesses.

levels.headline: Bank of England expected to raise Bank Rate on 5 November after inflation hits 3.5%

The Bank's main interest rate is 3.75%. It aims to keep inflation at 2%. When the Bank last met in September, six of its nine rate-setters voted to hold, and three voted to raise the rate to 4%. Underlying inflation, which leaves out food and energy, also went up to 2.8%. Petrol and diesel were almost 30% dearer than a year before.
Traders in financial markets now think a rise next month is almost certain. Another could follow in December.

The Bank's main rate is now 3.75%. In September, six of its nine decision-makers voted to leave it alone, but three wanted a rise to 4%. Petrol and diesel prices have jumped by nearly 30% over the year, partly because of the conflict involving Iran.
Investors think the Bank will raise rates next month, and maybe again in December. That would make borrowing, such as mortgages, more expensive, but could help to slow price rises.

levels.headline: Bank of England likely to raise interest rates after inflation jump

Why? Prices are rising faster. This is called inflation. It reached 3.5% in September, but the Bank wants it to be only 2%. Petrol and diesel are nearly 30% more expensive than last year, partly because of war in the Middle East.
When interest rates go up, borrowing costs more, so people tend to spend less, and prices can calm down. But it can also mean higher bills for people with mortgages. Savers may get a little more.

levels.why: It matters because higher interest rates can make loans cost more, but may slow rising prices.

levels.why: It matters because higher interest rates can make loans cost more, but may slow rising prices.

levels.headline: Interest rates in Britain may go up
levels.body:

Interest is a small extra charge when you borrow. When the Bank pulls the lever up, borrowing costs more. People then buy a little less, so prices stop rising so fast. It is like telling a bouncy playground to calm down.

headline: Healey's first Budget on 28 October faces tight finances and expensive borrowing

terms.meaning: The margin by which the government meets its own borrowing rules; more headroom means more room to spend or cut taxes.
Bonds issued by the UK government to borrow money.

levels.headline: Healey's first Budget on 28 October faces tight finances and expensive borrowing
levels.body:
Chancellor John Healey will deliver the first Autumn Budget of Andy Burnham's government on 28 October, with little room for manoeuvre. CNBC reported in early October that the pair had not yet set out the full mix of savings or tax measures needed to pay for extra spending while sticking to the UK's fiscal rules.
Burnham has refused to rule out tax rises, and British press reports suggest a windfall tax on banks could be considered. Britain now has the highest government borrowing costs in the G7, with the 10-year gilt yield recently around 5.34%. Weak growth is narrowing the government's fiscal headroom.
Former Bank of England chief economist Andy Haldane warned the UK is on thin ice and should show it is willing to cut spending to calm investors, while cautioning against targeting businesses.
levels.why: The Budget sets taxes and spending, so it affects household bills, public services and what it costs the government to borrow.

The 10-year gilt yield was recently about 5.34%. Slow economic growth means less headroom, the gap between the government's plans and its own borrowing limits.
Andy Haldane, a former Bank of England chief economist, said the UK is on thin ice. He argued ministers should show willingness to cut spending, but should avoid targeting businesses.

levels.headline: A big money speech is coming
levels.body:
The Budget is a big speech about money. The Chancellor, John Healey, will give it on 28 October. He will say what taxes people and firms will pay, and what the government will spend money on, such as hospitals and schools.
This Budget is hard. The government wants to spend more, but borrowing money costs a lot at the moment. Britain pays more than any other rich country in a group called the G7. The economy is also growing only a little.
The Prime Minister, Andy Burnham, has not promised that taxes will stay the same. Newspapers say banks might be asked to pay more. An expert warned that Britain is on thin ice, meaning it must be careful.
levels.why: It matters because the Budget decides what people pay in tax and what the government spends.

levels.headline: A big money speech is coming
levels.body:
The Budget is when the person in charge of money tells the country the plan. In Britain this person is called the Chancellor. Right now it is John Healey. His speech is on 28 October. He will say what people pay in tax and what the government spends.
But the pot of money is small right now. Borrowing costs a lot, and the economy is growing slowly. It is like trying to plan a school trip when the bus costs more than you hoped.
So the Chancellor may have to choose between raising taxes and spending less. The Prime Minister, Andy Burnham, has not ruled out higher taxes. People are waiting to see what he decides.
levels.why: It matters because the Budget decides what people pay in tax and what the government spends.

levels.headline: A big money speech is coming
levels.body:
Imagine a class is planning a school party. The teacher has a small pot of money, and everything costs more than last year. She must decide what to buy and whether to ask for more money from everyone. The Chancellor, John Healey, has a job a bit like that.
On 28 October he will give a big speech called the Budget. He will tell the country how the government will get money, from taxes, and how it will spend it. This is the first Budget for the Prime Minister, Andy Burnham.
Money is tight, so the grown-ups may have hard choices. Some people may pay more tax. We will find out on 28 October.
levels.why: It matters because the Budget decides what people pay in tax and what the government spends.

headline: UK government approves drilling at Jackdaw North Sea gas field despite environmental concerns

terms.meaning: An area under the sea off Britain from which natural gas is pumped to the surface.
Supplies of oil and gas that can still be taken from the ground.

levels.headline: UK government approves drilling at Jackdaw North Sea gas field despite environmental concerns
levels.body:
The UK government approved drilling at the Jackdaw gas field in the North Sea on 21 October, a decision environmental campaigners have criticised, Euronews reported. Prime Minister Andy Burnham defended the move, saying it is right to look in a responsible way at maximising the energy reserves Britain already has.
The approval comes while energy costs are weighing on households and businesses. UK inflation rose to 3.5% in September, with motor fuel prices 29.8% higher than a year earlier, which analysts link to the conflict involving the United States and Iran and disruption around the Strait of Hormuz. Britain is a net energy importer and so exposed to such shocks.
CNBC reported in July that US President Donald Trump had welcomed Burnham's plan to speed up oil and gas exploration in the North Sea.
levels.why: It shows the tension between keeping energy supplies and bills under control and meeting climate goals.

headline: Brent crude settles at $113.17, highest since May, on reports of fresh US and Israeli plans for Iran strikes

terms.meaning: The international benchmark price for oil, quoted per barrel.
A narrow sea passage between Iran and Oman through which a large share of the world's oil is shipped.

levels.headline: Brent crude settles at $113.17, highest since May, on reports of fresh US and Israeli plans for Iran strikes
levels.body:
Brent crude, the international oil benchmark, rose 4% on Thursday 22 October to settle at $113.17 a barrel, its highest close since May. CNBC linked the jump to reports of possible renewed US and Israeli strikes on Iran.
Unnamed US officials told the New York Times that the two militaries have drawn up plans for strikes after the November midterm elections. President Donald Trump said he is not negotiating with Iran and that something one way or the other will happen fairly soon, without giving details. The US has also ordered non-emergency staff out of Saudi Arabia, citing Houthi attacks, and Tehran said seven oil tankers caught fire or were damaged in the Strait of Hormuz on Thursday.
Higher oil prices feed straight into petrol, diesel and inflation. UK motor fuel prices were already 29.8% higher than a year earlier in September.
levels.why: Oil prices feed into petrol, heating and food costs, so they influence inflation and interest rates around the world.

headline: Macron condemns 'stupid' comments on French protests as 10-year borrowing cost tops 5%

terms.meaning: The interest rate a government pays to borrow; it rises when investors worry about lending to it.
A government that does not have enough seats in parliament to pass laws without help from other parties.

levels.headline: Macron condemns 'stupid' comments on French protests as 10-year borrowing cost tops 5%
levels.body:
French President Emmanuel Macron criticised what he called unacceptable and even stupid comments by foreign leaders about unrest in France, saying he was referring to Donald Trump among others. Speaking in Doha, Macron also denied that foreign interference caused the unrest. Trump had claimed France was under siege, looted and set ablaze by migrants, jihadists and communists.
The unrest followed peaceful demonstrations by trade unions, Yellow Vest protesters and students that were marred by looting and clashes with police. Several city centres have imposed curfews, and extra security is planned for protests on Saturday 24 October.
France's 10-year bond yield briefly crossed 5% on Wednesday for the first time since 2002. On Thursday it hit 5.113%, above the 10-year US Treasury yield for the first time since 2013. Investors are watching whether Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu's minority government can pass the 2027 budget.
levels.why: Unrest in a major economy can raise borrowing costs across Europe and test the stability of governments.

headline: Russia strikes Kyiv with cluster-warhead missiles hours after US envoy Witkoff meets Putin

terms.meaning: A missile warhead that splits in mid-air and scatters many smaller explosives over a wide area.
A person sent by a government to carry out talks on its behalf.

levels.headline: Russia strikes Kyiv with cluster-warhead missiles hours after US envoy Witkoff meets Putin
levels.body:
Russia struck Kyiv with three ballistic missiles carrying cluster warheads, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said, hours after US envoy Steve Witkoff met Vladimir Putin in St Petersburg. One missile hit Pechersk, the historic centre of the city. Zelenskyy said the weapon and the target were chosen deliberately.
At least two people were killed and 34 were injured, including five children. Zelenskyy said Russia fired 21 missiles in total during three waves of ballistic strikes on Kyiv.
Witkoff described his talks with Putin as constructive but said important work remained. He drew heavy criticism for calling Putin a humanitarian, although the Russian president is wanted by the International Criminal Court over the alleged deportation of Ukrainian children. Reports noted that Kyiv was not part of the talks, and US officials denied claims that Witkoff and Kushner threatened to withdraw support unless Ukraine made concessions.
levels.why: Peace efforts and attacks on civilians shape the security of Europe, energy prices and the support allies give Ukraine.

levels.headline: Italy's truckers' fuel protests leave shelves empty and airports short of fuel

Crotone and Reggio Calabria airports ran out of aviation fuel. Police have identified 1,339 people and issued 242 administrative fines, and the government has warned of criminal charges.
On Thursday the Meloni government approved a decree-law with urgent support for road haulage, farming and fishing, including €60 million for farm fuel. Matteo Salvini said more than €1 billion has been made available to transport. Some drivers have resumed deliveries, but the protest has not fully ended.

levels.headline: World's largest wealth fund posts $30 billion third-quarter loss as bonds fall
levels.body:
Norway's sovereign wealth fund, run by Norges Bank Investment Management (NBIM), reported an accounting loss of 278 billion kroner, about $29.7 billion, for the third quarter of 2026. CNBC described it as the world's largest wealth fund, with around $2.3 trillion in assets, although Euronews put its size at about €2.1 trillion.
The fund's overall return was -0.5%. Its bond holdings, known as fixed income, fell 3.5%, while its shares gained 0.5%. NBIM said government bond yields rose in the quarter to levels not seen since the financial crisis, and bond prices fall when yields rise.
Deputy chief executive Trond Grande said the fund's return was close to flat, ending slightly negative as rising interest rates led to weaker results on fixed-income investments.
